title: Four ways to water a garden
word: Four ways to water a garden
hookLine: Teresa: prayer can be like carrying buckets, a water wheel, a stream, or rain

lines: TERESA OF ÁVILA WRITES IT DOWN.
cards: A Carmelite nun in Spain is asked by her confessors to write down how she prays. Her name is Teresa, from the city of Ávila. She isn't a trained theologian, and she says so.

So instead of a system, she reaches for a garden. Someone is handed a patch of hard, weedy ground and told to make it grow. In her account, the Lord has already pulled up the weeds and put in good plants.
The job left is water. And there are, she says, four ways to get it there.

teach.b: First: you draw water from a well by hand and carry it in buckets. Heavy, slow, and some days the well seems dry.
Teresa says this is how prayer often begins: effort, attention, gathering a wandering mind, again and again.
Second: a water wheel, turned by a crank, lifting many buckets at once. Less sweat, more water. Prayer grows quieter; the soul rests a little, and something is given that you didn't haul up yourself.
Third: a stream running through the garden. Now the gardener mostly guides where the water goes. Fourth: rain.
The gardener does nothing at all.

teach.h: THE GARDENER WORKS LESS, GOD GIVES MORE.
teach.b: As the ways go on, the gardener works less and the Lord gives more. Teresa doesn't call the buckets a failure. They're where she says people begin, and she's frank that she spent long, dry years there herself.
Back on day one hundred six, a dry prayer still counted; her buckets are that same dry work. She doesn't promise the steps come in a neat line, either. The garden can go back to buckets.
Psalm sixty-five has a line for her fourth way: "Thou visitest the earth, and waterest it." And Paul, of his own work: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase."
This has been a week of letting go: Lady Poverty, perfect joy in the cold, brother sun and sister water, an instrument of peace, a life that preaches, Elijah in the hush.
Teresa adds her own: keep carrying the bucket, and leave the rain to God.

how: Teresa's image of the four waters is taught in Carmelite houses and retreats as a way to describe the growth of prayer, from effortful meditation toward quieter prayer received as gift.

games.q: you're Teresa's gardener, and the well seems dry. nothing comes up for days. what does she say?
o: keep carrying the bucket and leave the rain to God.
dig a new well somewhere else.
games.why: Teresa knew dry years. her advice is to keep at the work that's yours and trust the giving to the Lord.

practice: Ask honestly which picture fits your prayer, or your inner life, right now: buckets, hard work and not much coming up; a wheel, some rhythm; a stream, things moving on their own; or rain, something given you didn't earn.
There's no right answer and no grade, so just name it. If you pray, you can tell God which one it is today; if you don't, simply notice the dry places and the wet ones.

wordCard.voice: Four ways to water a garden. Teresa of Ávila's picture of prayer: buckets, a wheel, a stream, and rain, with less of our work and more of God's as it goes.

carryVoice: Your line: sometimes buckets, sometimes rain. Hauling water is no proof you're doing it wrong. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.
